flags.heading: A Missing Ciborium
flags.text: During Holy Mass on 25 March 1907, the Feast of the Annunciation, Father Fernando Gomez, pastor of the Church of Our Lady of the Angels in Silla, Spain, went to the tabernacle to bring out the Hosts for the distribution of Communion — and found the tabernacle door already standing open, the silver ciborium and its consecrated Hosts gone.

flags.heading: Recovered Beneath a Rock
flags.text: Two days later, the missing Hosts were found in a small garden on the outskirts of the city, concealed beneath a rock where the thief, or thieves, had apparently left them.

flags.heading: Examined and Sealed
flags.text: In 1934, the Hosts were formally examined and found, in the words of the resulting report, to remain "in the same state in which they were recovered under the rock and maintained their original condition unaltered."

flags.heading: A Document Lost to Fire
flags.text: Two years later, in 1936, the Archbishop's palace was burned down amid the anticlerical violence of the Spanish Civil War, and the formal documentation of the case was lost in the fire along with much else.

flags.heading: A Document Lost to Fire
flags.text: It was not until 1982, on the 75th anniversary of the original theft, that Archbishop Miguel Roca of Valencia undertook a new canonical process and formally authorized public veneration of the Hosts.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Hosts remain today in the tabernacle of the Church of Our Lady of the Angels in Silla, placed in a new reliquary for veneration on the tradition's centenary in 2007 and carried in procession to mark the occasion.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Silla's account, like the earlier Onil tradition from the same region of Spain, rests its case less on any single dramatic event than on simple, sustained physical preservation — a theft, a recovery, and then more than a century of a relic that has never shown the decay bread of its kind would ordinarily undergo.

flags.heading: A Host That Would Not Fall
flags.text: Tradition holds that before it could land, the Host rose back up on its own and came to rest gently on the corporal spread beneath the paten, in full view of the congregation.

flags.heading: The Bishop's Own Testimony
flags.text:
Word of the sign reached Thomas de Cantimpré, a Dominican friar, doctor of theology, and suffragan Bishop of Cambrai, who traveled to Douai to examine the matter personally and later recorded his own testimony in his theological work Bonum universale de Apibus:
"I saw the face of Christ crowned with thorns, with two drops of Blood."

flags.heading: A Devotion That Outlived a Revolution
flags.text: By 1356, just a century after the event, the church of St. Amatus was already keeping a regular weekly devotion to the relic; the church itself was destroyed during the French Revolution, but not before a canon of the collegiate church of St. Peter, sensing the danger, removed the Host, placed it in a small wooden box, and hid it beneath the Altar of the Dead, leaving with it a note in Latin identifying the relic for whoever might one day find it.

flags.heading: Rediscovered After Sixty Years
flags.text: The box remained hidden for over sixty years, until 1854, when the pastor of St. Peter's discovered it during work beneath the altar; inside was a small Host, still white, together with the canon's original note dated 5 January 1793, asking that the relic be preserved for the faithful of the future.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Host remains venerated today at the Collegiate Church of St. Peter in Douai, where the faithful still gather every Thursday of the month in prayer before it — a devotion that has now survived, by the town's own reckoning, a medieval accident, a revolution, and sixty years of quiet concealment beneath an altar built for the dead.

flags.heading: A Church Built Like a Tomb
flags.text: The Basilica of St. Stephen at Neuvy-Saint-Sépulcre, in the Indre region of central France, was founded in the early eleventh century by a lord named Eudes de Déols on his return from his own pilgrimage to Jerusalem, and was deliberately built on the round plan of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre — a design intended to let French pilgrims unable to make the journey themselves still walk, in miniature, the same sacred ground.

flags.heading: A Cardinal's Gift
flags.text: On 15 July 1257, Cardinal Eudes of Châteauroux, returning from the Crusades in the Holy Land, presented the church with two drops of what tradition holds is Christ's own Blood, gathered at Calvary during the Passion, together with a fragment of his tomb.

flags.heading: Blood Kept Pure
flags.text: The relic is described in the church's own tradition as coagulated but pure, uncontaminated by water or earth in its gathering — a detail the community has long held to distinguish it from other Precious Blood relics venerated elsewhere in medieval Europe, several of which carry more disputed or contested accounts of their own origin.

flags.heading: Indulgences and an Unbroken Devotion
flags.text: In 1621 the Archbishop of Bourges, André Frémiot, founded a Confraternity of the Most Precious Blood at Neuvy, and two years later Pope Gregory XV granted new indulgences to those who honored the relic there; the parish still keeps Easter Monday and the first of July each year as days of solemn Mass and procession in the relic's honor.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: What can be said with confidence is that this particular relic has been venerated continuously at Neuvy-Saint-Sépulcre since a cardinal's own hand delivered it there in 1257 — a devotion that has now outlasted, by more than seven and a half centuries, the very age of Crusade and pilgrimage that first carried it the length of Christendom to reach its resting place.

flags.heading: A Chronicle's Account
flags.text: According to a French chronicle written some decades after the fact, on Easter Sunday, 2 April 1290, a Christian woman of Paris pawned a consecrated Host, along with some of her own clothing, to a Jewish moneylender named Jonathas in exchange for a loan.

flags.heading: A Chronicle's Account
flags.text: The chronicle holds that Jonathas then subjected the Host to a series of violent tests — piercing it, throwing it into a fire from which it is said to have risen unburned, and finally plunging it into boiling water, from which it is said to have emerged in the shape of a small crucifix.

flags.heading: A Documented Trial, a Contested Legend
flags.text: Historical records independently confirm that a Jewish man was tried and executed in Paris in 1290 on a charge of desecrating a Host, and that his confiscated house passed to the French crown.

flags.heading: A Documented Trial, a Contested Legend
flags.text: The specific miraculous elements of the story, however, appear only in hagiographic accounts written decades afterward, and historians studying the episode have long noted that it stands among the earliest fully documented instances of a host-desecration accusation leveled against a Jewish community in medieval Europe — a charge that would recur, with tragic consequences, across the continent for the following two centuries.

flags.heading: A Chapel on the Confiscated Site
flags.text: King Philip IV recorded the confiscation of Jonathas's house in a deed of sale in 1291 and granted the site to a Paris burgher, who built a chapel there; Pope Boniface VIII issued a bull on 17 July 1295 authorizing its foundation, and the chapel, consecrated in 1299, became known popularly as the House of Miracles, with the street itself taking on the nickname Rue du Dieu bouilli — "the Street of the Boiled God."

flags.heading: A Name That Outlasted the Legend
flags.text: The chapel passed through several religious communities over the following centuries and became known as the Church of the Billettes, the name it still carries in the Marais district of Paris; the relic itself, kept for generations in a small reliquary at the nearby church of Saint-Jean, was lost during the French Revolution and has never been recovered.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: This entry, in keeping with the Church's own obligation of honesty about a difficult history, does not treat the medieval identification of Jonathas's guilt, or the miraculous details later attached to his trial, as settled historical fact — and asks that the account be received as part of a genuinely painful chapter of Christian-Jewish history, inseparable from the violence such accusations helped to justify across medieval Europe, rather than as an uncomplicated devotional celebration.

flags.heading: A Fallen Particle
flags.text: On Easter Sunday, 31 March 1331, at the first Mass of the day in the small village of Blanot in Burgundy, the parish vicar, Hugues de la Baume, was distributing Communion when a small particle of the Host fell unnoticed from the mouth of a widow named Jacquette, landing on the linen cloth the altar servers held beneath the hands of each communicant.

flags.heading: "The Body of Our Lord Fell"
flags.text:
An altar server assisting at the Mass, Thomas Caillot, caught what the priest had not and called him back to the rail, saying:
"Father, you must return to the rail because the Body of Our Lord fell from the mouth of this lady onto the cloth."

flags.heading: A Stain That Would Not Wash Out
flags.text: The priest attempted repeatedly to wash the stain from the cloth, but each attempt only left the mark darker and larger, and the water in his basin itself turned bloody; unable to remove it by any means, he cut the stained square from the larger cloth and declared before the assembled congregation, in words later recorded, that this was the Precious Blood of Christ.

flags.heading: An Investigation and Two Papal Confirmations
flags.text: The Bishop of Autun, Pierre Bertrand, opened a formal inquiry into the events soon afterward, interviewing the witnesses present at the Mass; the resulting documentation was sent to Pope John XXII, who confirmed the sign as a genuine Eucharistic miracle.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The stained cloth was hidden by nuns and parishioners through the upheavals of the French Revolution and returned to the church once the danger had passed; an eighteenth-century examination by the Bishop of Autun found the blood still bright red and the cloth itself undecayed after hundreds of years.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: It remains today in a crystal reliquary at the parish church of Blanot, still solemnly exposed each year on the feast of Corpus Christi, nearly seven centuries after one small, unnoticed fall from a widow's mouth.

flags.heading: A Monstrance Bought Secondhand
flags.text: In 1430, a woman in Monaco purchased a monstrance from a secondhand dealer, unaware — or perhaps only later realizing — that it still contained a large consecrated Host, almost certainly because the vessel itself had been stolen from a church.

flags.heading: A Knife and Living Blood
flags.text: As she did, living Blood is said to have begun flowing from it, drying almost immediately and leaving behind, imprinted on the Host itself, an image of Christ seated on a throne, flanked by instruments of his Passion.

flags.heading: From a Frightened Woman to a Pope
flags.text: Unsettled by what she had done, the woman brought the Host to a local canon named Anelon, who kept it in his own care; word of the event spread quickly enough to reach Pope Eugene IV, who arranged for the Host to be given to Duke Philip of Burgundy.

flags.heading: Three and a Half Centuries, Then Fire
flags.text: The Host remained intact and venerated at Dijon for more than 350 years — a span of continuous devotion unusually long even among Eucharistic relics of this era — until the French Revolution reached the city.

flags.heading: Three and a Half Centuries, Then Fire
flags.text: On 9 February 1794, revolutionary authorities requisitioned the basilica to consecrate it as a temple to the cult of Reason, and the miraculous Host, along with much else the Revolution regarded as superstition, was destroyed.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Though the relic itself did not survive, its memory did: numerous period documents and works of art record the event, including a stained-glass window in Dijon Cathedral that still depicts the central scene of a startled woman, a knife, and an image that appeared where none had been painted.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Dijon account stands as a reminder that even relics venerated across many generations are not guaranteed permanence — that devotion sometimes has to be content with memory alone, once the object itself has been lost.

flags.heading: Two Centuries of Perpetual Adoration
flags.text: The Chapel of the Holy Cross in Avignon, France, home to a Franciscan confraternity known as the Gray Penitents, had maintained perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament for some two hundred years by the time of the events of 1433 — a devotion tracing back to a solemn act of reparation organized by King Louis VIII after his victory over the Albigensian heretics, who had denied the Real Presence.

flags.heading: A City Under Water
flags.text: After days of relentless rain in late November 1433, the Sorgue and Rhone rivers rose to a dangerous height and finally broke their banks, flooding the low-lying chapel, which stood directly along the Sorgue's course.

flags.heading: A City Under Water
flags.text: Convinced that the small church, and the Host exposed within it for adoration, must have been swept away entirely, the head of the confraternity and another friar set out by rowboat to reach the site.

flags.heading: A Dry Path to the Altar
flags.text: Reaching the chapel proved difficult through the floodwaters, but when the two friars finally arrived and made their way inside, they found the water risen to a height of some four feet throughout the building — except around the altar itself, where the floodwater had parted to either side, leaving the altar and the monstrance holding the Host completely dry.

flags.heading: A Song for the Parting Waters
flags.text: News of what the friars had found spread rapidly through the city, and crowds gathered at the chapel to witness the scene for themselves, several hundred people by the accounts that survive.

flags.heading: A Song for the Parting Waters
flags.text: In gratitude, the confraternity established an annual commemoration on 30 November, the feast of St. Andrew, at which the brothers still sing, before Benediction, verses from the Canticle of Moses composed after the parting of the Red Sea.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Avignon account belongs to a small category of Eucharistic tradition built not around blood or transformation but around simple, physical preservation — the Host and the ground immediately around it spared from a flood that reached everything else in the building.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Nearly six centuries later, the Gray Penitents still gather each 30 November at the Chapelle des Penitents Gris to mark the anniversary, carrying forward a devotion that has, by their own telling, already survived one flood it should not have.

flags.heading: A Boy Who Could Not Speak
flags.text: Bertrand had been paralyzed and mute since a serious fall five years earlier, at the age of seven, and had never fully recovered the use of his body or his voice.

flags.heading: A Priest's Hesitation
flags.text: The parish priest initially refused, since Bertrand's muteness made it impossible for him to make a sacramental confession beforehand — but the boy persisted in his silent pleading until the priest, moved by his evident sincerity, relented and gave him Communion.

flags.heading: A Sudden and Complete Cure
flags.text: From the moment the Host touched his tongue, Bertrand felt himself seized by what witnesses described as a mysterious force, and within moments his paralysis lifted entirely and his voice returned.

flags.heading: A Sudden and Complete Cure
flags.text: According to the manuscript account compiled afterward, his very first words, spoken for the first time in five years, were drawn from Scripture: 'Our help is in the name of the Lord.'

flags.heading: A Church Already Marked by Relics
flags.text: The healing took place in a church that already held its own relic of note — two drops of Christ's Blood, brought from the Holy Land in 1257 and preserved there for two centuries before Bertrand's cure.

flags.heading: A Church Already Marked by Relics
flags.text: The most authoritative surviving account of the 1461 healing is a painted manuscript still kept today in the Cathedral of La Rochelle, offering an unusually direct visual record of an event otherwise known only through later retelling.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The La Rochelle account belongs to a smaller category of Eucharistic tradition centered not on a transformation of the bread and wine but on healing granted at the moment of reception itself — the sacrament working, as the faithful understood it, exactly as it claimed to.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Whatever a modern reader makes of a five-century-old cure, the manuscript that recorded it, and the persistence of a mute boy who refused to be turned away from Communion, together preserve a story about insistence rewarded rather than fabricated for effect.

flags.heading: A Theft in Deep Winter
flags.text: In the last days of December 1532, thieves broke into the parish church of Marseille-en-Beauvaisis, in northern France, and made off with a silver-gilt ciborium holding a number of consecrated Hosts.

flags.heading: A Stone Untouched by Snow
flags.text: On New Year's Day 1533, a resident named Jean Moucque was making his way down the same street through a driving blast of wind and snow when his attention was caught by something unusual: a single stone lying in the open, exposed to the full force of the storm, that had not gathered a single flake of snow on its surface while everything around it lay buried.

flags.heading: A Chapel and a Healing
flags.text: A chapel — the Chapelle des Saintes-Hosties, still standing today beside the parish church — was raised soon afterward to encourage devotion at the site, and several healings were subsequently attributed to prayer there, most notably that of a paralyzed priest named Jacques Sauvage, who was reportedly cured completely.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Marseille-en-Beauvaisis account joins a substantial body of medieval and early modern tradition built around Hosts abandoned by thieves and preserved against every natural expectation — in this case, not fire or flood but simple exposure to a winter storm the stone itself seemed mysteriously spared.

flags.heading: Three Days of Exposition
flags.text: In 1608, the Benedictine monks of the abbey at Faverney, in the Franche-Comte region of France, had papal permission to expose the Blessed Sacrament for three days of public veneration around the feast of Pentecost.

flags.heading: Three Days of Exposition
flags.text: On the eve of the feast, 24 May, they set two Hosts in a large monstrance on a provisional altar of repose and left two oil lamps burning before it overnight.

flags.heading: A Church Full of Smoke
flags.text: Early the next morning the sacristan, Dom Garnier, opened the church doors to find it filled with smoke, the provisional altar already engulfed in flames that would go on to reduce it entirely to ashes, melting even a nearby metal chandelier with the heat.

flags.heading: Suspended Above the Ruins
flags.text: As the fire was finally brought under control and the smoke began to clear, a young novice named Hudelot noticed something the older monks had missed in the chaos: the monstrance itself, holding both Hosts, was hovering in midair above the wreckage of the altar, unsupported by anything beneath it, leaning gently toward the grille at the back where the altar had stood.

flags.heading: A Vigil of Thirty-Three Hours
flags.text: Unsure how to respond, the monks summoned Capuchin friars from nearby Vesoul, who built a new altar directly beneath the suspended monstrance and celebrated Mass; at the moment of elevation, the monstrance descended slowly on its own to rest on the new altar, having remained aloft for some thirty-three hours in all.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Archbishop of Besancon declared the event authentic on 10 July 1608, and Pope Paul V granted a bull of indulgence later that same year after the miracle was reported to Rome.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: One of the two Hosts was later transferred to Dole for safekeeping and was destroyed in the French Revolution, but the second survives and remains venerated at Faverney today, carried each year in the same monstrance — rebuilt after the original's own destruction in the Revolution — that first held it suspended above a burning altar four centuries ago.

flags.heading: A Chalice Set Aside
flags.text: Afterward, following custom, he placed the chalice — which still held a consecrated Host — back in its repository near an altar dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, and the townspeople returned to their ordinary work for the day.

flags.heading: Fire Near the Altar
flags.text: Parishioners rushed back to the church in alarm once the flames were discovered, but by the time the fire was brought under control, the chalice itself had been completely consumed — reduced, along with much of the altar area, to ash and melted metal.

flags.heading: A Host Beneath a Tin Bubble
flags.text: Searching through the wreckage afterward, those clearing the site found that only the foot of the chalice had survived the heat at all, and that a small bubble of tin had formed beneath it during the fire — sealing within it the consecrated Host, which was found completely intact and undamaged when the bubble was opened.

flags.heading: Consumed the Next Day
flags.text: The Host recovered from beneath the melted metal was consumed the following day, in keeping with ordinary practice for a consecrated Host too small a quantity to preserve indefinitely as a standing relic.

flags.heading: Consumed the Next Day
flags.text: What survived instead was the documentary record of the event and, notably, a set of stained-glass windows in the church of Pressac depicting the different stages of the fire and its aftermath.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Pressac account belongs to the same broad family as Bagno di Romagna, Faverney, and several other fire-related Eucharistic traditions from this period — a consecrated Host surviving heat that destroyed the vessel meant to protect it.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: What the windows of Pressac preserve, centuries after the Host itself was consumed, is not a relic but a record: an image, in colored glass, of a fire that took everything around the altar except the one thing the parish most needed to remain.

flags.heading: The Octave of Corpus Christi
flags.text: On 2 June 1668, the Saturday within the octave of Corpus Christi, the pastor of the small church of Les Ulmes, in France, Father Nicolas Nezan, exposed the Blessed Sacrament for public adoration and began incensing the monstrance as the faithful sang the hymn Pange Lingua.

flags.heading: A Figure in Place of the Host
flags.text: As the singing reached the verse 'Verbum caro panem verum' — 'the Word made flesh, true bread' — those present reported that the Host itself seemed to give way to the shape of a man: light-brown hair falling to his shoulders, a luminous face, hands crossed over one another, and a white tunic covering the figure entirely.

flags.heading: A Vision Witnessed by All
flags.text: The apparition lasted, by the accounts of those present, for roughly a quarter of an hour, witnessed not by one or two individuals but by the whole congregation gathered for the adoration.

flags.heading: Recognized and Preserved
flags.text: After examining the testimony, the bishop authorized devotion to the event, and the Host associated with it remained enshrined in a specially built recess in the church for more than 130 years — a recess still visible in the church today.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The parish of Les Ulmes kept the anniversary of the apparition as a solemn annual observance well into the following centuries, and the event received renewed scholarly attention at the International Eucharistic Congress of Angers in 1901 and again at the National Eucharistic Congress of 1933, where a full session was devoted to studying the 1668 account.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: An old print depicting the vision, along with the empty recess that once held the Host itself, remain the parish's lasting physical connection to an event witnessed, by every surviving account, by an entire congregation at once.
